prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms removes motional and light-shift perturbations, and for its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B055 (the experimental Higgs discovery) to B012 with Katori and Ye. My view of the science has not moved: the 2012 observation is the clearest clue from nature in a generation, and I still think the experimental discovery deserves a prize. What changed is the attribution problem, which round 1 showed to be unresolved by our own files. Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce accept the physics but none can defend a trio, and the trios named in this committee differ (mine, Lindroth's and the chair's). A prize whose credit we cannot justify to the community is not one I can vote for, because our process is to find the discovery first and then the people behind it, and here the second step fails under a three-name limit across ATLAS and CMS. B012 passes both steps. The magic-wavelength lattice lets thousands of atoms be interrogated while Doppler, recoil and first-order light shifts are suppressed, and that is what took optical clocks from about 10^-16 to 10^-18. The result has been reproduced and compared at that level by independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE). It already gives millimetre-scale gravitational redshift in the laboratory and a sharpened search for drifting constants and ultralight dark matter. Answering the chair's first question, the distinction from 2005 and 2012 is that the comb supplied the means to count optical cycles and the ion work supplied single-particle quantum control, whereas the lattice is a separate idea that makes a many-atom ensemble unperturbed, and the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime and not clocks in general. On the chair's third question I do not require the redefinition of the second or a detection of new physics before awarding: the demonstrated, cross-checked performance is a measured fact, and waiting for a signal that may never come would punish a null result.
statement.case_against: The honest case against B012 is that it is a refinement of a programme already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and that its headline fundamental-physics payoff is still prospective: no variation of constants and no dark-matter signal has been seen. I ranked it seventh at opening for exactly that reason, because I want a clue from nature and not only a better ruler, and I have not fully lost that reservation. Credit also extends beyond two names (Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Bloom and groups at PTB, NIST and SYRTE), and ion clocks reached comparable accuracy by another route. Finally, I am giving up a candidate I believe is more consequential for physics as a whole, and a committee that wants the most important discovery and not the cleanest case could fairly say I have traded significance for defensibility. If external experts report that priority within the lattice-clock community cannot be reduced to Katori and Ye, B012 loses the advantage that moved me, and I would reopen the question.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube first to B012 first after the opening ballots, but warns that B012 attracts consensus in part because it offends nobody, and he left B055 out of his configuration because the Higgs allocation cannot be defended.
responses.response: I accept your attribution point on the Higgs, and it is what moved me, not a head count. I also accept your warning, and I do not want to vote for B012 merely because it is comfortable. My reason is positive: it is a quantitatively controlled measurement with independent confirmation and a concrete route to tests of general relativity and of constants. I would still ask you to keep IceCube alive. Your own caveat that the source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) are modest in number matches my view that B013 is maturing and not yet mature, so I would not put it forward now, but it should stay a standing candidate and I list it as an alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the magic-wavelength lattice is a different idea from the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion control, and that it is what moved the field from about 10^-16 to 10^-18, while she defers to Mark and me on the Higgs and declines to trade clean attribution for a more famous topic.
responses.response: This answers the question I put to you in round 1, and it satisfies me: the comb counts optical cycles, the ion work controls one particle, and the lattice makes an ensemble unperturbed, so the novelty is real and lies in the idea and not only in the instrument. I draw one consequence for the wording. The citation must name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime, and I would keep the fundamental-physics payoff out of the operative clause, since it is prospective and your own file lists it as a caveat. I still disagree mildly on one point: the Higgs is not merely more famous, it is the clue from nature the Standard Model was waiting for. But I agree that fame cannot substitute for a defensible allocation of credit.

responses.point: Kroll says the Higgs has full scientific weight and maturity but that any trio looks like a compromise, and he would reconsider B055 only if the committee settles the individual allocation. He also asks whether Katori and Ye are the right two names given Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups.
responses.response: I agree that Higgs allocation has not been settled, and I do not see it being settled by argument among us, since our trios differ and Della Negra's claim is as strong as any. So I stop pressing it. On your question about Katori and Ye I am less sure than I sound in my own statement: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength idea and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye drove it to 10^-18 with many-body control, which is a coherent two-name story, but I rely on memory and agree that an external report on priority (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) should be obtained before the vote is final. I share your inclination that the measured 10^-18 performance is enough and the redefinition of the second need not be awaited.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B018 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a mature theory-plus-experiment case distinct from 2016, but says he would accept B012 if the topological case fails to reach agreement, and acknowledges that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission and the 3D strand cannot be handled in three names.
responses.response: I think your own reservation decides it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe and sit outside the trio, Zhang's death makes the omission permanent, and the 3D Fu-Kane-Mele-Moore-Balents strand cannot fit in three names, so B018 has the same kind of allocation problem that has led me away from the Higgs. I do not dispute that the Z2 topological insulator is a new class of quantum matter with decades of confirmation, and I keep B018 in mind as a strong candidate if a defensible credit can be written. Since you say you would accept B012 as the fallback and I now prefer it, I would ask you to say what citation wording or external report would make that acceptance firm.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names for the lattice clock: I rely on memory for the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and I would want the external expert reports on priority before the final ballot.

Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I believe it is, because the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate idea, but a colleague could reasonably call it a refinement.

Whether the Higgs discovery should be honoured at all through individuals; if the committee finds a defensible allocation, B055 would return to the front of my list, and the lack of a prize for the experimental discovery is a real cost of passing it over.

Whether the first results on constants, redshift tests or dark matter, or the redefinition of the second, will change the weighting of B012 over the next few years; I treat them as future support and not as a condition.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My ties are to David Gross (PhD supervisor), Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string-theory group, and none is connected to Katori, Ye or any other shortlisted candidate. My own work on dark bubble cosmology and horizonless black-hole mimickers touches B027 only indirectly, and B027 is not in my configuration. As Secretary I would be the one commissioning expert reports, and I have no stake in what they say about lattice-clock priority.
